I Asked AWS DevOps Agent for a Monthly Audit. It Found a Plaintext Password.

One chat, one read-only tool, and a cron trigger. Here is how I built a custom agent that audits my AWS account on the 1st of every month, what it found on the first run, and where it was honest about what it couldn’t see.

// 01

Why I wanted a monthly audit

I have one AWS account that runs a bit of everything: a business website, an LMS with a Bedrock knowledge base, my portfolio, a couple of small APIs and a pile of lab experiments. Nothing checks it regularly. I wanted something that would, without building yet another Lambda, EventBridge and SNS contraption.

AWS DevOps Agent is usually pitched for incidents: triage, root cause analysis, that sort of thing. It also lets you build custom agents with their own prompt, tools and triggers. So I described the audit I wanted in chat and let it build one.

Setup happens once. After that, the cron trigger fires every month, the agent runs read-only checks across us-east-1 and ap-south-1 plus global services, and the results go three places.

// 02

Creating an AWS DevOps Agent agent space

An agent space sets what the agent can see and do. I named mine Recommendations and left the description and response language empty.

For resource access I let the console auto-create the primary account role. The content safety guardrail is on by default, and I left it on.

The toggle worth understanding is Agent Actions. It lets the agent change resources, and every change waits for explicit approval. My auditor only uses read-only calls, but this is where that switch lives.

A third role covers the web app, which opens through an IAM session. For a lab account, the AWS owned encryption key is fine.

RoleWhat it is for
DevOpsAgentRole-AgentSpace-…Read access to resources in the primary account
DevOpsAgentActionsRole-AgentSpace-…Approved write actions, only if Agent Actions is on
DevOpsAgentRole-WebappAdmin-…Opening the web app through an IAM session
// 03

Connecting Slack to AWS DevOps Agent

Integrations are called capability providers. There are 19: cloud, pipeline and telemetry tools. Register a provider once and every agent space in the account can use it.

Slack is three steps: start the install, pick a workspace (not an Enterprise Grid org), approve the app.

Then the agent space needs a channel. Paste the channel ID from Slack’s channel details and invite the app. Bidirectional mode, where the agent reads and replies to channel messages, was off when I set this up.

// 04

A tour of the web app

From the agent spaces list, Launch via IAM opens the web app. My older EC2 agent space sits right below the new one.

Agents lists the managed ones AWS maintains: learning, chat, incident triage and incident RCA. Knowledge holds instructions, skills and memories. Managed memory stores stay empty until there are real investigations to learn from.

Settings shows the ARN, guardrail status and usage hours. Access tokens connect Claude Code, Kiro, A2A or other agent spaces over MCP, disabled until an admin turns them on. The chat box has Smart, Balanced and Fast modes plus a thinking level; I stayed on Balanced, High.

// 05

Letting it learn my topology

As soon as the space exists, the agent starts mapping the account. AWS says up to 30 minutes.

The summary report described my account better than I would have, including a fair point that live workloads and lab experiments share one account.

Topology groups resources into applications, and each one drills down.

// 06

Building a custom agent through chat

Agents has a Custom tab with three ways in: a form, a chat, or importing a system prompt from a Markdown file in a connected repo. I picked chat. It asked three questions.

This is exactly what I typed back, typos included:

I asked for Lambda, CloudFront and VPC, and told it to go deeper based on my topology. Instead of guessing, it surveyed what was running in both regions first.

Last round: IAM Identity Center, DynamoDB, Organizations, and always report to Slack.

AreaWhat it checks
EC2IMDSv2 enforced (HttpTokens: required), unencrypted EBS
IAMUsers without MFA, unused users and keys (90+ days), root MFA, broad trust policies
IAM Identity CenterPermission sets, group and account assignment changes
Security groups / VPC0.0.0.0/0 on 22, 3389 and database ports; VPC flow logs
S3, RDS, DynamoDBPublic access, encryption, backups
Lambda, CloudFrontSecrets in environment variables, runtimes, WAF, TLS policy
OrganizationsSCPs, member accounts
// 07

The custom agent: one tool and a cron trigger

A system prompt that reads like something I’d write, one tool (use_aws, read-only), no skills, no memory stores. Scheduled straight away.

Cron, because rate expressions can’t do monthly:

cron(0 9 1 * ? *)   # 09:00 UTC on the 1st of every month
// 08

The part where it doubted itself

When I asked it to always report to Slack, the agent checked its toolbox, found no Slack-posting tool, and said it couldn’t confirm the channel ID matched the channel I named.

It worked anyway. Posting comes from the agent space’s Slack association, so the custom agent never needs a Slack tool. I could also tag the bot in the channel and ask about the account.

// 09

The first monthly audit run

I didn’t want to wait for the 1st, so I ran it manually. Slack got a run-started message, then the full summary in the thread.

Thirteen recommendations came out of that run, each tagged with the agent that created it and waiting for review.

// 10

What the AWS security audit found

// critical

An ADMIN_PASSWORD stored in plaintext in a Lambda function’s environment variables.

That alone justified the hour. If you find one, rotate it first, then move it to Secrets Manager or a SecureString in Parameter Store and read it at runtime.

SeverityAreaFinding
CriticalLambdaADMIN_PASSWORD in plaintext environment variables
HighSecurity groups5 groups expose SSH (22) to 0.0.0.0/0; more allow all traffic, including both default SGs
HighIAM2 CodePipeline roles trust the account root
HighIAM2 CloudFormation roles with IAMFullAccess plus PowerUserAccess
HighOrganizationsZero custom SCPs
HighOrganizationsNew member account joined with no access review
HighCloudFrontNo WAF web ACL on enabled distributions
MediumVPCFlow logs off in both regions

On the numbers: the first run created 13 recommendations, later runs added more as I widened scope, which is why the report says 17.

It reported its own blind spots

The auto-created role couldn’t read MFA devices, access keys, the account summary or Identity Center permission sets. Instead of skipping those checks quietly, the agent raised them as a finding, listed manual checks for now, and gave the permissions to add.

PermissionCheck it unblocks
iam:ListMFADevicesMFA on IAM users
iam:ListAccessKeysKey age and rotation
iam:GetAccountSummaryRoot MFA (AccountMFAEnabled)
sso-admin:DescribePermissionSet and friendsWhat a permission set actually grants
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Action": [
    "iam:ListMFADevices",
    "iam:ListAccessKeys",
    "iam:GetAccountSummary",
    "sso-admin:DescribePermissionSet",
    "sso-admin:ListManagedPoliciesInPermissionSet",
    "sso-admin:GetInlinePolicyForPermissionSet",
    "sso-admin:ListAccountAssignmentsForPrincipal"
  ],
  "Resource": "*"
}
// 11

Reports, skills and GitHub

I wanted a PDF. The agent checked its own docs with verify_aws_claim and said plainly there is no PDF or HTML export for custom agent output. The closest thing is an Artifact, so I asked for one every run.

Skills extend the agent without touching its prompt: a form, chat, a zip with SKILL.md, or a repo. I loaded my cost comparator skill to see how it would handle it.

To import from my own repos I connected GitHub through the GitHub App, read-only.

Importing a skill is a directory URL containing a SKILL.md.

// 12

Bonus: a diagram from one prompt

The agent already knew my topology, so I asked it to describe the architecture, then asked for a diagram.

It left out the ap-south-1 copy of the visitor counter because it isn’t on the request path. That’s a call I’d expect from a person.

// 13

Notes if you try this yourself

  • Name the regions and services in your first message. The agent fills the gaps well, but it surveys what you point it at.
  • Add the IAM and sso-admin read permissions to the agent space role before the first scheduled run, or MFA and key checks come back as gaps.
  • Set up the Slack channel on the agent space first. Posting comes from that association, not from a tool on the custom agent.
  • Run it manually once instead of waiting for the 1st.
  • There is no PDF export for custom agent output. Ask for an Artifact report on every run.
  • Counts differ between Slack, the chart and the Artifact as runs accumulate. Quote one source.
  • Recommendations include role names, account IDs and usernames. Blur before you share screenshots.
// 14

FAQ: AWS DevOps Agent custom agents

Can AWS DevOps Agent run a custom agent on a schedule?

Yes. A custom agent can have triggers, including a cron expression. Mine uses cron(0 9 1 * ? *) to run at 09:00 UTC on the 1st of every month. Rate expressions can’t express monthly.

How does a custom agent post results to Slack?

Through the agent space’s Slack association. You register Slack as a capability provider, associate the agent space with a channel ID, and run summaries arrive there. The custom agent itself only needed the use_aws tool.

Can I export custom agent output as a PDF?

Not directly. When I asked, the agent confirmed there is no PDF or HTML export for custom agent output. The closest option is an Artifact report that lives in the agent space.

What permissions does the audit need?

The auto-created agent space role covers most read calls, but mine was missing iam:ListMFADevices, iam:ListAccessKeys, iam:GetAccountSummary and several sso-admin read actions. Add them so MFA, access key and Identity Center checks run fully.

Does the agent change anything in my account?

Not this one. It only makes read-only use_aws calls. Agent Actions can make changes, but every change requires explicit approval before it runs.
